articles.content:
Everyone's calling PhotoCraft a Photoshop clone or dismissing it as AI slop. After putting it to work, I think they're missing what makes it different.

In this video, I connect an AI agent to PhotoCraft and use prompts to edit a layered image, change backgrounds, and work with masks and effects. You'll see what works, what needs manual cleanup, and why this workflow has me switching photo editors.

I also investigate the project's development, revisit a bug I reported, and test whether the latest release actually fixes it.

Covered in this video:
- AI-assisted editing with live previews in PhotoCraft
- Working with layers, masks, backgrounds, and shadows
- Where automation helps and where manual editing still matters
- Development activity, community contributions, and bug fixes
- Why I think PhotoCraft deserves more than a quick Photoshop comparison

articles.title: He Built CentOS Linux. Now He Wants Truly Open AI.
articles.author: Chris Titus Tech
articles.summary: What if we built AI like Linux? Downloading a model doesn't tell you what went into making it, and bigger models aren't always better. I sit down with Greg Kurtzer, founder of CentOS, to discuss what truly open-source AI could look like. Greg shares his work on Open Waldo, his experience training mo
articles.content:
What if we built AI like Linux? Downloading a model doesn't tell you what went into making it, and bigger models aren't always better.

I sit down with Greg Kurtzer, founder of CentOS, to discuss what truly open-source AI could look like. Greg shares his work on Open Waldo, his experience training models on his own hardware, and why scaling up actually made one of his models worse.

We explore smaller local models, transparent training data, privacy, copyright, and the security risks of AI agents. We also discuss how the Linux and open-source communities can help make AI more accessible.
CentOS was my first Linux distribution, so this conversation meant a lot to me. It also left me wanting to build my own model.
What would you train a local AI model to do?

articles.content:
Is AI doom about protecting the public, protecting profits, or a little of both?

I break down the incentives behind AI fear, why companies like OpenAI and Anthropic might welcome regulation, and how cheaper open-weight and local models could challenge their business models.

We also look at real AI risks, questions about independent evaluations, and why an AI bubble bursting could hurt far more than tech companies. Some of these connections are speculation, not proven facts, but they're worth examining alongside the doom-and-gloom headlines.

articles.content:
Everyone seems to be hyping Omarchy. I'm not switching to it, but some of its ideas are absolutely worth stealing.

In this hands-on review, I dig into DHH's take on Arch Linux and Hyprland: the plugins, polished theming, helpful menus, and opinionated defaults. I cover what impressed me, what I'd remove, and why my own desktop takes a different direction.

Then I show my Fedora setup with DWM, X11, and Quickshell, including the ideas Omarchy inspired me to bring into my own workflow.

That's the beauty of Linux: keep what you like, change what you don't, and build something that works for YOU.

Which Omarchy feature would you steal for your own desktop? Let me know in the comments.

articles.title: I Rebuilt My Entire Website in Astro… Was It Worth It?
articles.author: Chris Titus Tech
articles.summary: I rebuilt my entire website from Hugo to Astro after years of using Hugo as the backbone of ChrisTitus.com. Hugo was fast, simple, and honestly still fantastic—but my site had grown into much more than a blog. Downloads, livestream archives, chat replay, forums, search, store integrations, and other
articles.content:
I rebuilt my entire website from Hugo to Astro after years of using Hugo as the backbone of ChrisTitus.com. Hugo was fast, simple, and honestly still fantastic—but my site had grown into much more than a blog. Downloads, livestream archives, chat replay, forums, search, store integrations, and other features were starting to push Hugo beyond what I wanted it to do.

In this video, I break down why I moved to Astro, what the massive migration looked like, how I used AI review loops to help with the conversion, and what Astro gives me that Hugo didn't. I also cover the downsides: Astro has a much heavier Node/npm ecosystem, requires more security and CI checks, and the migration even appears to have reduced my AdSense revenue.
Was it worth it? For my site, absolutely. But if you're running a straightforward static blog, I'd still recommend Hugo.

Thanks to Blacksmith for sponsoring this video. I’ve been using their GitHub Actions runners and caching to significantly reduce CI build times.
